subject_title: Evaluation and Assurance of ML, LLM, and Nondeterministic Systems
theoretical_foundations:
AI assurance is an evidence problem over a socio-technical system, not a single accuracy score. Testing asks whether an implementation behaves as specified under controlled conditions; evaluation estimates performance or risk against tasks, scenarios, or reference populations; verification checks that the implemented data, model, configuration, and measurement procedure conform to specified requirements; validation asks whether those requirements and the observed behavior are sufficient for the intended use and operating context. The distinction is consequential: a model can be verified against its training pipeline yet fail validation because the construct is wrong, the deployment population differs, or human workflow changes the outcome. NIST AI RMF 1.0 organizes assurance within GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE and treats validity/reliability, safety, security/resilience, transparency/accountability, explainability, privacy, and fairness as interdependent characteristics. It is voluntary and use-case agnostic, so an organization must make risk appetite, affected populations, operating limits, and go/no-go thresholds explicit.

An evaluation should begin with an estimand rather than a metric. Let Y_ir be the scored outcome for benchmark item i and repeated trial r under a declared model, prompt, decoding, tool/retrieval, and environment version. A benchmark-conditional estimand is performance on the fixed released items; a generalized estimand is expected performance over a defined superpopulation of similar future items. These are different claims. NIST AI 800-3 shows that benchmark and generalized accuracy can differ and require different uncertainty calculations. For nondeterministic systems, repetitions quantify output variance but do not create independent items: trials are clustered within items, users, sessions, and versions. A design should therefore sample both items and trials, report per-item pass probability and aggregate estimates, and use cluster/bootstrap or hierarchical methods that preserve the dependence structure. Sources of uncertainty include item sampling, annotation disagreement, user and context variability, random seeds/decoding, provider/model updates, and model or benchmark selection.

Task and risk taxonomies provide coverage. Tasks may be closed-form (exact answer or executable test), structured prediction (classification, ranking, extraction), open-ended generation (quality, factuality, groundedness, style), or human-in-the-loop outcomes (utility, comprehension, decision quality). Risk dimensions should be mapped to the intended context: validity and reliability; safety and harmful content; fairness and representativeness; privacy and memorization/PII leakage; security and adversarial manipulation; information integrity/provenance; intellectual-property and value-chain risk; calibration, over-reliance, and abstention; and environmental or operational cost. Lifecycle coverage should include data collection and labeling, pretraining/fine-tuning or retrieval, release, deployment, monitoring, incident response, and decommissioning. The taxonomy must not imply that a passing score on one risk is evidence for another.

Construct validity asks whether a proxy measures the concept claimed (for example, whether an LLM judge score measures grounded correctness rather than stylistic fluency); internal validity asks whether a measured difference is attributable to the model rather than prompt, sample, evaluator, or confound; external validity asks whether results transport to the intended population, time, language, workflow, and stakes. Reliability is repeatability of measurement, not truth. Calibration is agreement between confidence and empirical correctness; a confident wrong answer is a calibration failure even when mean accuracy is acceptable. Selective prediction makes uncertainty operational: choose a coverage level and measure risk on answered cases, abstention quality, and escalation latency/cost.

For generative systems, automatic text overlap metrics are narrow indicators, not universal quality measures. Deterministic checks are valuable for schemas, citations, code execution, numerical answers, policy constraints, and prohibited content; semantic and factual claims need reference-grounded checks, domain experts, or structured human ratings. Human evaluation can estimate preference or task utility, but raters require a representative sampling frame, training and anchored rubrics, blinded randomized presentation, consent and protections where applicable, adjudication, inter-rater reliability, and explicit treatment of disagreement. LLM-as-judge can reduce cost and increase iteration speed, but it is a measurement instrument that needs calibration against blinded humans, prompt and model version control, position randomization, verbosity/style controls, judge diversity, sensitivity analysis, and periodic revalidation. Agreement with humans on one benchmark does not establish general validity; circularity, self-preference, position, verbosity, and judge drift remain plausible.

Risk evidence should combine model testing, adversarial/red-team testing, and field or user testing. Security assurance covers evasion, poisoning, privacy attacks, extraction, backdoors, and generative misuse; for an LLM application it also covers prompt injection, untrusted retrieval content, PII exfiltration, and unsafe output handling, without treating a conventional tool-using agent trajectory as this module's subject. Robustness evaluation perturbs inputs, domains, languages, formats, and operating conditions and reports degradation and recovery, not just clean-set scores. Fairness evaluation disaggregates quality, false-positive/false-negative, calibration, abstention, and exposure-to-harm measures by relevant groups and intersections, with uncertainty and small-cell safeguards; group parity metrics are context-dependent and may conflict. Privacy evaluation includes training-data memorization, membership/inference or extraction attempts, logging and retention, and release of evaluation artifacts. Toxicity and harm evaluation needs severity, context, prevalence, attack success, false-refusal, and residual-risk measures rather than one binary rate.

Benchmark validity is an engineered property. A benchmark record should state its construct, task protocol, sampling frame, inclusion/exclusion rules, labels and adjudication, subgroup and language coverage, temporal window, preprocessing, scoring code, known errors, licensing, contamination threat model, and intended claims. Keep development, tuning, and sequestered holdout data separate; split by entity, time, conversation, source, or near-duplicate cluster when random splitting would leak information. Audit exact, n-gram, semantic, synthetic-data, and post-release overlap where feasible, and disclose uncertainty when model training data are inaccessible. Use immutable manifests, content hashes, semantic versions, change logs, anchor items, and a comparability record so a score remains attached to the benchmark release, prompt, evaluator, and runtime. Static public tests invite optimization and eventual contamination; dynamic or private items improve freshness but reduce reproducibility and can introduce new labeling bias, so maintain stable anchors plus rotating challenge sets.

Statistical assurance requires prespecified metrics, sample-size/power or precision targets, paired comparisons where the same items are used, confidence or credible intervals, effect sizes, multiple-comparison control, and sequential-monitoring rules. Use Wilson or exact intervals for simple proportions when appropriate; cluster bootstrap over items/users for repeated generation; mixed-effects or generalized linear mixed models when item difficulty, model effects, language, domain, and trial variance matter; and reliability statistics for human ratings. Report both point estimates and uncertainty, not p-values alone, and do not count repeated trials as independent evidence. For model selection, use non-inferiority/equivalence or lower-confidence-bound gates when a safety or fairness threshold matters, plus explicit abstain/escalate behavior. Statistical significance is not practical significance, and a narrow interval around a biased or invalid construct is still bad assurance.

In an enterprise SDLC, trace each requirement and risk to a test/evaluation block, an owner, an evidence artifact, a threshold or decision rule, and a post-deployment check. Store raw prompts/inputs, outputs, scores, annotations, seeds/decoding settings, model and provider IDs, retrieval corpus version, evaluator version, and hashes subject to privacy controls. Use independent review for high-impact decisions, a red-team issue taxonomy, canary or shadow release, drift and shift monitors, calibrated alerts, rollback or model replacement, and feedback channels for users and affected communities. A production result is evidence about the tested configuration and sampling process, not a permanent property of a model family. NIST's 2026 TEVV-Athlon Initial Public Draft proposes four stages—Articulate & Organize; Define & Construct; Apply & Measure; Synthesize & Interrogate—using customizable Events, Tools, and measurement Blocks. It is useful as a design pattern, but its status is draft (public comment opened August 7, 2026 and closes October 6, 2026), not a finalized certification standard.

Contested claims and evidence gaps should be visible. NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 23894, and the GenAI Profile are guidance rather than proof of safety; model cards and datasheets improve traceability but cannot guarantee representativeness or truthful disclosure. HELM demonstrates the value of standardized multi-metric reporting and a living benchmark, yet no benchmark can cover an open-ended deployment. The MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena study reported over 80% judge-human agreement for its setting while also documenting judge biases and largely not measuring safety; transfer to other languages, domains, or high-stakes harms is unproven. GLMMs can improve precision when their assumptions fit, but their extra assumptions are themselves a validation obligation. Long-tail harm rates, longitudinal causal impact, black-box privacy measurement, multilingual/cultural coverage, and validity of synthetic/dynamic benchmarks remain active research gaps.
practical_architecture_and_implementatio:
Use an assurance package with six linked records. (1) System and context record: intended and prohibited uses, users and affected groups, stakes, operating envelope, human oversight, fallback/abstention, model/provider/version, prompt and retrieval configuration, data provenance, and legal/ethical constraints. (2) Risk and requirement register: map each risk to likelihood, severity, affected population, control, residual-risk tolerance, owner, and evidence. Use NIST GOVERN/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE and ISO/IEC 23894 as adaptable organizing structures; do not treat either as a universal scoring formula. (3) Benchmark/dataset card: define construct and estimand, sampling frame and representativeness, label process, subgroup/intersection coverage, temporal and language slices, known errors, licenses, leakage/contamination checks, release/hash/version, and whether items are public, private, rotating, or synthetic. (4) Evaluation protocol: prespecify test items, trial count, decoding and environment controls, randomization, baselines, metrics, acceptance rules, uncertainty method, missing/abstained output handling, and multiplicity/sequential rules. (5) Evidence ledger: immutable raw inputs/outputs, annotations, metric results, confidence intervals, judge prompts and model IDs, security findings, reviewer sign-offs, and reproducibility metadata. (6) Decision/feedback record: release decision, exceptions, compensating controls, incident links, monitoring thresholds, rollback, and next-review date.

A minimum experiment architecture for an LLM or statistical model has a sequestered holdout, a development set, and a production-like field set. Split by user/entity/source/time or near-duplicate cluster, not merely rows, when correlation or leakage is plausible. Maintain stable anchor items for longitudinal comparability and rotate fresh/private challenge items for contamination resistance. Before scoring, hash and normalize inputs for exact/near-duplicate checks; test semantic overlap and synthetic-data provenance where feasible; record training-data disclosure limitations. Evaluate a fixed model configuration with at least enough independent items to meet a precision target and repeat stochastic generation per item under declared seed/temperature/top-p settings. Analyze results with item-level clustering or a GLMM; report benchmark-conditional and generalized claims separately. For paired model comparisons, use identical items, randomized output order, paired intervals, and practical equivalence/non-inferiority bounds.

Metric selection should be a portfolio. For classifiers, report prevalence-aware precision/recall, F1, AUROC and especially PR-AUC for imbalance, confusion matrices, subgroup errors, and calibrated probabilities. For regressors, report MAE/RMSE or task-cost loss with prediction-interval coverage. For ranking/recommendation, report relevant utility and exposure or harm slices. For generation, combine deterministic validity/schema/execution tests, citation or retrieval-grounded factual checks, task-specific rubric dimensions, semantic similarity only where justified, toxicity/harm severity, refusal and false-refusal rates, latency/cost, and human/LLM-judge ratings. For confidence, report reliability diagrams, Brier/NLL, expected calibration error with bin sensitivity, and selective risk-versus-coverage curves. For fairness, predefine group membership handling, minimum cell sizes, uncertainty, intersectional slices, and which error or allocation harms matter. For robustness, create perturbation and distribution-shift strata and report worst-slice or quantile degradation. For privacy/security, measure PII leakage, memorization/extraction, prompt-injection or evasion success, attack budgets, false positives, and recovery.

Human-evaluation service: sample tasks from the intended use distribution; recruit raters who represent relevant users or domain expertise; blind model identity and randomize answer order; train with rubric examples; include gold or adjudication cases; collect free-text rationales only when useful; calculate agreement/reliability and disagreement distributions; and route severe safety, privacy, discrimination, or self-harm content to trained reviewers. Validate any LLM judge as an instrument by freezing prompt/rubric/model version, calibrating on a stratified human-labeled set, measuring agreement and bias by task/group/length, randomizing pair position, testing judge-model swaps, and retaining a human audit sample. Prefer pairwise or rubric dimension scores over an unexplained scalar; combine deterministic checks for objective dimensions and humans for consequential or ambiguous judgments. Treat judge explanations as audit clues, not proof of reasoning.

Red-team service: derive attack families from the threat model and NIST adversarial-ML taxonomy; include benign boundary cases, adaptive and multi-turn prompts, indirect untrusted content, multilingual and low-context variants, and realistic misuse incentives. Version prompts and attack tools, randomize where appropriate, log attack budget and stopping rules, score severity-weighted harm and attack success, include false-refusal and usability costs, and obtain independent review. Convert each finding into a reproducible regression test with a mitigation, owner, due date, residual-risk decision, and retest. A static prompt list is a seed corpus, not evidence of robustness.

Production feedback loop: deploy with a canary/shadow phase; monitor quality, calibration, abstention, drift/shift, safety/harm, fairness slices, privacy/security alerts, latency/cost, human override and appeal rates, and user-reported failures. Separate data drift (P(X)), label/prior drift (P(Y)), concept drift (P(Y|X)), provider/model/prompt changes, and workflow/population changes. Establish alert thresholds with uncertainty and minimum sample counts, investigate slice-specific regressions, and define rollback, rate limits, human escalation, retraining or re-evaluation triggers. Re-run the pre-release suite after any model, prompt, retrieval corpus, evaluator, policy, or provider change; preserve anchors and annotate benchmark revisions. Feed incidents and affected-community feedback into new risk hypotheses and tests.

Three implementation gates are practical: evidence completeness (all intended-use claims have traceable tests and limitations), statistical adequacy (estimands, dependence, uncertainty, power/precision, and multiple comparisons are documented), and risk acceptability (residual harm/security/privacy/fairness is below the approved context-specific tolerance, with safe failure and abstention). A failed gate should lead to narrowing use, adding controls or human review, recalibration, rollback, or no-go—not silent metric substitution. Keep the module boundary explicit: evaluate ML/LLM model and application behavior, including retrieval and output handling, but do not claim coverage of multi-tool agent trajectory/control evaluation.

primary_evidence.source_title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Elham Tabassi; National Institute of Standards and Technology
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: The Framework is intended to be voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector specific, and use-case agnostic.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This is normative scope language, not a certification claim. In an SDLC it supports tailoring risk-based evidence to context while requiring the organization to document its own risk tolerance, governance, measurement, and management decisions. The Core's MEASURE function explicitly calls for rigorous testing, uncertainty, benchmarks, formal reporting, independent review, and regular in-operation evaluation; trustworthiness characteristics are interdependent and trade-offs require human judgment.

primary_evidence.source_title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: This document defines risks that are novel to or exacerbated by the use of GAI.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The profile operationalizes AI RMF for generative systems and identifies confabulation, harmful bias/homogenization, dangerous or hateful content, information integrity, data privacy, security, intellectual property, value-chain integration, and human-AI configuration risks. Its suggested actions require use-case-appropriate benchmarks, contamination disclosures, fairness slices and affected-community input, PII detection, provenance checks, adversarial testing, real-world testing, and feedback integrated into metrics. It is guidance, and the profile itself notes that future revisions may add risks and actions as empirical evidence develops.

primary_evidence.source_title: Expanding the AI Evaluation Toolbox with Statistical Models (NIST AI 800-3)
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Drew Keller, Kweku Kwegyir-Aggrey, Ryan Steed, Anita K. Rao, Julia L. Sharp, A. Stevie Bergman; National Institute of Standards and Technology
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Benchmark and generalized accuracy may meaningfully differ and therefore must be calculated in different ways.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This report provides direct statistical guidance for nondeterministic evaluation. It defines benchmark accuracy conditional on fixed items versus generalized accuracy over a superpopulation, warns that simple standard errors can be invalid, and demonstrates generalized linear mixed models on 22 API-access LLMs and three benchmarks. In an enterprise gate, state which estimand is being claimed, model item difficulty and trial/item clustering when needed, report uncertainty, and treat GLMM assumptions and diagnostics as part of validation rather than assuming the method is universally better.

primary_evidence.source_title: The TEVV-Athlon Framework for Evaluating AI Systems (NIST AI 200-2 ipd)
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: P. Jonathon Phillips, Theodore Jensen, Patrick Hall, Razvan Amironesei, Yee-Yin Choong, Craig Greenberg, Kristen K. Greene; National Institute of Standards and Technology
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: This paper introduces the TEVV-Athlon Framework, a four-stage method for developing customized assessments of AI systems.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: Status must be preserved: this is the August 2026 Initial Public Draft, released for a 60-day public comment period from August 7 through October 6, 2026, and not a finalized standard or certification. Its four stages—Articulate & Organize, Define & Construct, Apply & Measure, and Synthesize & Interrogate—offer a practical architecture for translating organizational goals into Events, Tools, and evidence Blocks. The draft expressly spans statistical ML, LLM, multimodal, and agentic systems; this module uses its generic TEVV design pattern but excludes agent trajectory/control evaluation by scope.

primary_evidence.source_title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Assessment of the Robustness of Neural Networks — Part 1: Overview (ISO/IEC TR 24029-1:2021)
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: This document provides background about existing methods to assess the robustness of neural networks.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: As a technical report rather than a universal pass/fail test, it supports a robustness workstream: define perturbations and operating limits, test clean and shifted inputs, characterize degradation and recovery, and document method assumptions. Enterprise evaluators should extend this to text, multimodal, and generative settings and report which threats were and were not tested.

primary_evidence.source_title: Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Guidance on risk management (ISO/IEC 23894:2023)
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: The application of this guidance can be customized to any organization and its context.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: ISO/IEC 23894 provides a lifecycle risk-management frame for organizations developing, deploying, or using AI, but it intentionally does not supply a single metric or threshold. Use it to connect context, risk identification, analysis, treatment, monitoring, and records to the evaluation plan; justify tailoring and residual-risk decisions rather than presenting conformity as evidence that a model is fit for every use.

primary_evidence.source_title: Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (NIST AI 100-2e2023)
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Apostol Vassilev, Alina Oprea, Alie Fordyce, Hyrum Andersen; National Institute of Standards and Technology
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: The taxonomy is built on survey of the AML literature and is arranged in a conceptual hierarchy.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The taxonomy structures security evaluation by AI type, lifecycle attack stage, attacker goal, capability, knowledge, and data modality. Apply it to threat-model-driven red teaming and regression tests for evasion, poisoning, privacy, extraction, backdoors, and generative misuse. NIST also emphasizes limitations of mitigations; a defense claim needs an attack budget, threat assumptions, residual risk, and retest evidence rather than a one-time scan.

primary_evidence.source_title: The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness and Technical Debt Reduction
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Eric Breck, Shanqing Cai, Eric Nielsen, Michael Salib, D. Sculley
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Testing and monitoring are key considerations for ensuring the production-readiness of an ML system.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The IEEE paper's 28-test rubric makes an important engineering point: prediction behavior is difficult to specify a priori, so data tests, model-development tests, infrastructure tests, and monitoring tests complement ordinary software tests. Use it as a checklist seed, not as a universal maturity score; adapt checks to context, add statistical/risk evidence, and retain rollback, debuggability, and monitoring artifacts.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Margaret Mitchell, Simone Wu, Andrew Zaldivar, Parker Barnes, Lucy Vasserman, Ben Hutchinson, Elena Spitzer, Inioluwa Deborah Raji, Timnit Gebru
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: We recommend that released models be accompanied by documentation detailing their performance characteristics.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: Model cards establish a practical evidence interface: intended and prohibited uses, evaluation procedures, subgroup and intersectional performance, limitations, and ethical considerations. In 2026, make the card versioned and linked to dataset cards, benchmark manifests, raw evidence, model/provider hashes, and change history. Documentation improves discoverability and accountability but cannot repair biased sampling or validate an unfit construct.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Timnit Gebru, Jamie Morgenstern, Briana Vecchione, Jennifer Wortman Vaughan, Hanna Wallach, Hal Daumé III, Kate Crawford
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: The machine learning community currently has no standardized process for documenting datasets.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: A dataset datasheet is the provenance and validity companion to a model card: motivation, composition, collection, preprocessing, labels, intended and prohibited uses, maintenance, distribution, licensing, and ethical/legal concerns. For evaluation, add sampling frame, representativeness, subgroup coverage, temporal window, contamination controls, known label errors, immutable version/hash, and benchmark split lineage. A static datasheet must be maintained as the dataset and threat environment change.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Rishi Bommasani et al.; Center for Research on Foundation Models, Stanford University
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: HELM is a living benchmark for the community, continuously updated with new scenarios, metrics, and models.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: HELM demonstrates multi-scenario, multi-metric evaluation, standardized conditions, released raw prompts/completions, and explicit trade-offs instead of a single leaderboard number. It is a strong university research pattern for benchmark versioning and transparency, but its coverage and scenarios do not establish fitness for an organization's domain, safety case, or affected communities. Preserve anchors for comparability while adding private/rotating, use-case-specific tests.

primary_evidence.source_title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Lianmin Zheng et al.; University of California, Berkeley and collaborating universities
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: We examine the usage and limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks paper supplies evidence that a strong judge can approximate human preference in its tested setting, while documenting position, verbosity, self-enhancement, and reasoning limitations. A production judge must therefore be treated as a calibrated, versioned measurement instrument: randomize order, use a rubric and dimension scores, compare against blinded human labels, test judge swaps and prompt sensitivity, retain an audit sample, and avoid inferring factual correctness or safety from preference agreement.

primary_evidence.source_title: Assessing Risks and Impacts of AI (ARIA): Pilot Evaluation Report
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Razvan Amironesei, Afzal Godil, Craig Greenberg, Kristen Greene, Johnston Patrick Hall, Theodore Jensen, Jonathan Fiscus, Noah Schulman; National Institute of Standards and Technology
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: the three testing levels (model testing, red teaming, field testing)
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: NIST's ARIA pilot is a concrete mixed-method pattern: model testing probes component behavior, red teaming explores adversarial misuse, and field testing observes realistic interactions; dialogue annotation, tester questionnaires, and measurement trees connect observations to validity claims. The pilot was small (five organizations and seven applications), so it is evidence of an evaluation design, not proof that the method generalizes or that a deployment is safe.

failure_modes_and_antipatterns: Leaderboard or single-metric monoculture: optimizing one public score hides task, subgroup, calibration, safety, cost, and deployment trade-offs; require a metric portfolio and explicit claims.

Benchmark contamination and leakage: training, tuning, retrieval, prompt engineering, or evaluator exposure to test items inflates results; use entity/time/cluster splits, exact and semantic overlap audits, private or rotating items, and disclose unknown training-data provenance.

Random row splits across correlated entities: records from one person, source, conversation, patient, document, or time period appear in train and test; split at the entity/source/time/near-duplicate level and validate externally.

Pseudo-replication of stochastic outputs: treating repeated trials on the same item as independent samples creates falsely narrow intervals; model item, user, session, and trial clusters and report both item and trial variance.

Single-seed or single-provider evaluation: one decode, seed, API snapshot, prompt, or judge is mistaken for stable behavior; sample repeated runs, freeze and log configuration, test provider/model changes, and report sensitivity.

Proxy without construct validation: a convenient toxicity, helpfulness, fairness, truthfulness, or user-satisfaction score is treated as the construct itself; document construct, internal, external, and consequential validity and test alternative operationalizations.

Judge circularity and bias: the model grades its family, style, verbosity, or preferred answer; randomize position, blind identity, calibrate to representative humans, use multiple judges and deterministic checks, and audit judge drift.

Human agreement as universal validity: high rater agreement can reflect a narrow or poorly framed rubric; ensure sampling and domain expertise, report disagreement and reliability, and validate against actual task outcomes or affected-community perspectives.

Aggregate fairness only: overall performance masks intersectional or small-group harms and can reverse under subgroup conditioning; prespecify relevant slices, uncertainty and minimum-cell rules, and pair parity metrics with harm and quality-of-service analysis.

Confidence without calibration or abstention: a probability, verbal hedge, or judge score is interpreted as truth; calibrate on deployment-like data, measure selective risk/coverage, and define escalation and safe failure.

Clean-set robustness theater: a model passes ordinary tests but fails under temporal, linguistic, formatting, adversarial, low-context, or domain shifts; define operating limits, attack budgets, perturbation strata, worst-slice degradation, and retest after mitigation.

Red-team theater: a fixed public prompt list produces a passing report while attackers adapt; threat-model attack goals and capabilities, use adaptive and multilingual scenarios, severity-weight outcomes, convert findings to regression tests, and retest.

Privacy and security boundary omission: output quality is tested but logs, prompts, retrieval corpora, model updates, PII, extraction, and vendor access are not; include data-flow, retention, access, memorization/extraction, injection/evasion, and incident evidence.

Static documentation: a model card or datasheet is written once and becomes stale after model, prompt, corpus, benchmark, policy, or provider changes; use immutable versions, hashes, change logs, owners, review dates, and automated linkage to evidence.

Metric-gate substitution: when a safety/fairness/privacy metric is hard to measure, teams silently replace it with an easier proxy; record unmeasured risks and limitations, use qualitative evidence and expert/community review, and make residual uncertainty part of the go/no-go decision.

Overclaiming standards or research: voluntary NIST/ISO guidance, a checklist, a living benchmark, or one judge-human agreement result is presented as certification or universal fitness; state status, assumptions, applicability, and evidence gaps.

Production feedback blind spot: offline pass results are not connected to user reports, overrides, appeals, incidents, drift, or affected-community feedback; instrument those channels, define alert and rollback rules, and feed incidents into new evaluation hypotheses.

maturity_matrix.foundational: Inventory each ML/LLM system and intended use; define prohibited use and operating limits; maintain dataset and model cards; create development, sequestered holdout, and production-like test sets with leakage-aware splits; run deterministic contract/schema/quality tests plus repeated stochastic trials; report item-level results, basic confidence intervals, calibration, subgroup slices, abstention behavior, and known limitations; perform a small independent human review and threat-model red-team; log model/provider/prompt/data/evaluator versions; gate release on explicit risk-owner approval and safe fallback.
maturity_matrix.advanced: Trace AI RMF/ISO risk statements to measurable requirements and evidence Blocks; use versioned anchor plus rotating/private benchmarks, contamination and near-duplicate audits, temporal/external validation, distribution-shift and robustness suites, fairness/intersectional and privacy/security tests, and severity-weighted harm metrics. Prespecify estimands, precision/power, paired comparisons, multiplicity and sequential rules; use cluster bootstrap or mixed-effects/GLMM analysis for item/trial variance; calibrate LLM judges to blinded representative humans and audit position/verbosity/self-preference bias; run independent red-team and field/user testing; deploy canary/shadow monitoring with drift, quality, calibration, abstention, incident and appeal feedback tied to rollback/re-evaluation triggers.
maturity_matrix.expert_2026: Operate a continuous, evidence-centered assurance program: custom TEVV-Athlon-style assessments connect organizational goals and affected-community impacts to risk taxonomies, measurement constructs, Events, Tools, Blocks, estimands, uncertainty, and release decisions. Preserve benchmark comparability with immutable manifests, hashes, anchors, rotating contamination-resistant items, data/provenance and judge versioning, and public/private evidence boundaries. Use hierarchical statistical models with diagnostics, practical non-inferiority/equivalence gates, adaptive sampling for rare harms, independent assessors, domain experts, representative human and field evaluation, calibrated abstention and safe failure, and adversarial red-team regression. Treat provider/model/prompt/retrieval/evaluator changes as new configurations; continuously monitor shift, fairness, privacy, security, toxicity, factuality, calibration, user outcomes, overrides, appeals and incidents; automatically open evidence gaps, trigger rollback or narrowed use, and feed post-deployment findings back into benchmark/risk redesign. Label NIST AI 200-2 as an August 2026 Initial Public Draft (not final) and document where enterprise controls extend beyond it.
